papers.title: Escherichia coli siphovirus DH23 features unusual C12-C13-C6 symmetry of the neck complex and the lateral tail fibers branching from the central tail fiber
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages capable of propagating in host cells that have entered or are approaching the early stationary phase of growth (eSPI phages) are promising candidates for phage therapy as they may efficiently destroy slowly growing pathogen populations in vivo. Among the Escherichia coli phages, the eSPI phenotype is rare and the diversity of such phages is limited. Siphoviruses of the Dhillonvirus genus appear to offer an attractive platform for implementing host range management systems. We investigated the structure of the eSPI Dhillonvirus DH23 using cryo-electron microscopy and single-particle analysis and revealed that its adaptor protein connecting the dodecameric head portal to the hexamer ring of the tail termination protein forms a tridecameric (C13) ring rather than a dodecameric ring as in most known bacteriophages. Despite the presence of the putative lateral tail fiber (LTF) protein gene in the DH23 genome, the tail tip 3D density map showed no evidence of LTF attachment. Examination of 2D projection images of the flexible distal part of the central tail fiber (CTF) revealed a massive density from which the LTFs emanate, forming a branched CTF-LTF structure that was not seen in coliphages previously.

papers.title: Segmental Acceleration in Protein Condensates
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates are essential to cellular processes and organization, and are typically formed by weak, multivalent interactions among biomolecules, such as intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Because condensates are much more viscous than the surrounding solution, they are generally expected to slow protein motions. While the length-scale-dependent dynamics of IDPs in dilute and dense phases have been studied separately, a systematic comparison of how these dynamics change upon phase separation remains lacking. In this study, we use coarse-grained, explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations to compare the segmental dynamics between the dilute and dense phases of the low-complexity domain of the RNA-binding protein Fused in Sarcoma (FUS-LC) and compositionally similar model IDPs of different lengths. Short protein segments, contrary to expectation, relax faster within the condensate than in the dilute phase, whereas segments longer than about one-seventh of the chain relax more slowly. Our results suggest that this crossover arises because chain collapse in the dilute phase slows local relaxation, whereas neighboring chains in the condensate slow chain-scale relaxation. The dilute phase sets both the magnitude of the speed-up and the segment length up to which it extends: dilute-phase relaxation changes with chain length and interaction strength, whereas relaxation within the condensate, at a fixed protein concentration, does not. Slower water dynamics increase the speed-up, whereas removing water eliminates it. Overall, our results suggest that condensates slow global protein motions but accelerate local ones, which may help preserve the liquid-like nature of the condensate's interior.

papers.title: Modeling three-dimensional structures of flaviviral exoribonuclease-resistant RNAs by combining functional and computational analyses
papers.abstract: Exoribonuclease-resistant RNAs (xrRNAs) are non-coding RNAs used by viruses to evade host RNase-mediated degradation. In flaviviruses, xrRNAs are thought to share an unusual knot-like fold with the 5'-end threaded through a ring formed by a multi-helix junction and closed by a pseudoknot, but only a handful of high-resolution structures have been solved to date. We combined structure prediction tools with mutational analysis of RNase resistance to determine previously unsolved 3D structures of xrRNAs from the West Nile virus (WNV) and two dengue virus (DENV) serotypes. We first predicted possible pseudoknot structures computationally, then tested them by systematically mutating putatively pseudoknotted bases and assessing RNase resistance to discriminate between models. The successful pseudoknot models were used to predict 3D structures computationally, refining the models by identifying tertiary contacts at the threaded 5' end via another round of mutagenesis and RNase resistance testing. We found that all 3 xrRNAs shared the same threaded knot-like architecture as in experimentally solved flaviviral xrRNAs, with similar tertiary contacts generating an analogous hierarchy of interactions importance for RNase resistance, but the pseudoknot length varied considerably, from 8 pairs in WNV to 2 in DENV2. This work illustrates a powerful new approach for determining xrRNA structures that are hard to obtain by high-resolution experimental methods by integrating computational predictions with functional assays.

papers.title: Protein docking on DNA surfaces using de novo designed binders
papers.abstract: Positioning proteins on DNA-functionalized surfaces offers a way to organize catalytic, recognition and signaling activities across materials from synthetic particles to programmable nanostructures. However, site-specific attachment typically requires protein-oligonucleotide conjugation. Here we adapt a small, de novo designed protein that binds a six-base-pair sequence from one duplex face into a genetically encoded surface adapter. We define geometric constraints near blunt ends, hairpin loops and crossover junctions, and identify linker and site-spacing combinations that increase tandem cis-dimer affinity. In synthetic macrophage receptors, these dimers trigger phagocytosis of DNA-coated beads, preserve sensitivity to origami ligand spacing, and remain active after a 24-hour delay when DNA-conjugated receptors decline. We also design trans-dimers bridging neighboring origami helices to dock fluorescent proteins, enzymes, an antibody fragment and SpyCatcher cargo. Together, these design rules and binding modes establish a modular framework for genetically encoded protein-DNA interfacing that should generalize to new de novo binders.

papers.title: Molpylot: a shared workspace for human-AI collaboration in molecular simulation
papers.abstract: Rigorous biomolecular simulation requires a long chain of physical decisions across fragmented tools. Language-model agents offer to automate this work, yet current agents operate outside the scientist's environment, generating ad hoc scripts or files that are effortless to launch but laborious to inspect and verify. Here we introduce Molpylot, an interactive modeling platform that unifies structure preparation, molecular dynamics, specialist protocols and replica-aware analysis in a graphical workspace designed to be immediate for the scientist, while exposing that same live session to any language model through 256 typed, tested tools. Operating within this shared workspace, the agent executes routine tasks under built-in safeguards that catch physical inconsistencies, while scientific judgment stays with the scientist. Across 18 systems, including asymmetric membranes, quantum-parameterized metal sites, enhanced sampling and free-energy calculations, we show how agents and built-in checks streamline setup, quality control and trajectory analysis. Molpylot is free for noncommercial use.

papers.title: Transcriptional activation forms insulation boundaries through cohesin-independent decompaction and cohesin-dependent barrier formation
papers.abstract: How 3D genome structure regulates transcription has been intensely studied, but how transcription regulates 3D genome structure remains poorly understood. To elucidate this relationship, we integrate Region Capture Micro-C and simultaneous live-cell imaging of CTCF chromatin looping and inducible nascent transcription at the Fbn2 locus with 3D polymer modeling and perturbation experiments. We find that transcription activation induces cohesin-independent insulation boundary formation at the Fbn2 promoter, locus decompaction, and faster chromatin dynamics. We also show that transcriptional bursts interfere with CTCF loop formation in living cells. Using 3D polymer modeling to distinguish plausible mechanistic models, we find that transcription-induced gene body decompaction can explain increased mobility and cohesin-independent insulation, while a polymerase-associated barrier to loop extrusion can explain transcription-linked looping changes. Together, these results reveal cohesin-dependent and -independent mechanisms through which transcription can establish insulation and regulate 3D genome structure.

papers.title: Structural deformations of lipid bilayers around membrane proteins inform oligomerization type
papers.abstract: A functional definition of a membrane protein's structure is the three-dimensional arrangement of the polypeptide and the structure of the membrane around it. Biological membranes are composed of self-assembled lipid bilayers, with membrane proteins acting as inclusions that perturb this phase. These inclusions induce long-range changes in membrane structure and create an intrinsic, lipid-mediated driving force for membrane protein association. The question is how much different membrane protein folds shape their surrounding membrane to tune the affinity and specificity of this driving force. To investigate this, we conducted a computational study to evaluate whether different membrane protein oligomers exhibit characteristic membrane defects that indicate specificity in complexation. We performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of monomeric and oligomeric states of ten different channels and transporters in POPC bilayers and evaluated changes in membrane thickness, deformation energy, and lipid packing parameters. We found that all the proteins affect their surrounding membrane up to 3 nm from the protein surface. However, we observed larger defects at oligomeric interfaces for obligatory or structurally monomorphic complexes, suggesting that their oligomerization is partly driven by burial of membrane defects. In contrast, oligomers that adopt different quaternary structures across homologs show weaker perturbations at known binding interfaces, and larger perturbations at lipid-facing surfaces. Nevertheless, all systems show fewer membrane defects upon oligomerization, suggesting an underlying lipid-mediated driving force that each protein fold modulates to tune affinity via membrane-mediated oligomerization.

papers.title: Near-surface flight enhances thrust in an insect-inspired flapping-wing robot
papers.abstract: A number of semi-aquatic insects rapidly move across the water surface using interfacial flight. In this locomotion strategy, flapping wings generate thrust above the air-water interface while surface tension supports their weight. This close proximity to the air-water interface alters aerodynamic force generation through ground effect, potentially enhancing horizontal propulsion. Here, we demonstrate that near-surface flapping enhances horizontal thrust by up to 17% at shallow stroke-plane inclinations. Using a beetle-inspired flapping-wing robot, we systematically vary wing-surface distance (D/c, where D is the minimum trailing-edge-to-surface clearance during flapping, normalised by chord length c) and stroke plane inclination {beta} at Reynolds numbers of order 103. Locomotion experiments show increased acceleration and higher terminal velocity near the surface (D/c < 1) at shallow stroke plane angles ({beta} = 30{degrees} and 45{degrees}), while direct wind-tunnel force measurements confirm increased aerodynamic thrust, distinguishing this enhancement from changes in water-related resistance. Particle image velocimetry further reveals that near-surface flapping alters passive wing motion and surrounding flow, producing stronger backward-directed flow after stroke reversal and earlier leading-edge vortex development during the initial upstroke. These findings establish a configuration-dependent aerodynamic benefit of near-surface flapping, providing insight into insect-scale interfacial flight and opportunities for enhancing propulsion in bio-inspired robotic systems.

papers.title: Insights into Ice-Growth Inhibition and Hydration Ordering by the Ca2+-Dependent Antifreeze Protein MaIBP_RIV
papers.abstract: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) inhibit ice growth by binding to specific ice surfaces, although the molecular basis of this activity remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the ice-growth inhibition mechanism of the calcium-dependent antifreeze protein MaIBP_RIV from Marinomonas arctica using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. MaIBP_RIV exhibits stable binding to the primary prism and basal ice planes through its ice-binding surface (IBS), effectively suppressing ice growth. IBS binding to the secondary prism plane is weaker and only temporarily inhibits growth. In contrast, the non-ice-binding surface (non-IBS) is repelled by the growing ice front. Our results also explain that Ca2+; stabilises the IBS and essential for ice-growth inhibition, while removing Ca2+; reduces IBS flatness, which significantly impairs its ice-growth activity. Experimentally characterised mutations on IBS residues (S44Y, G63D, N65Y, and D87Y) result in continuous ice growth, consistent with their reduced antifreeze activity. Hydration analysis of water molecules around IBS and non-IBS suggests that, by decreasing the temperature from 300K to 240K, the water molecules around IBS show more ice-like ordering compared to those around the non-IBS.

papers.title: Isolating soluble, near-native, misfolded states and their functional characterization: A step towards high-resolution protein misfolding structures
papers.abstract: Proteins can misfold into soluble, near-native states that act as long-lived kinetic traps with aggregation independent biological consequences. A key step toward obtaining high-resolution structures of these states is the ability to isolate/purify them. Here, we show this is possible for the Escherichia coli protein pyruvate kinase (pykF) following refolding from chemical denaturant. After controlling for aggregates the refolded (treatment) ensemble exhibits a decrease in average specific activity relative to the untreated (natively folded) sample. Size exclusion chromatography reveals two distinct populations in this treatment group, whereas the untreated group exhibits a single population. Native PAGE analysis finds that both populations from the treatment group have the same mass and electrophoretic mobility as the untreated protein, consistent with native-like global properties and oligomerization state. Functional analysis using Michaelis-Menten kinetics shows that one population retains activity comparable to the untreated sample, while the other has no detectable activity, indicating that approximately 31 +/- 17.9% (95% Confidence Interval) of refolded molecules are soluble, near-native, but non-functional. ANS fluorescence measurements probing hydrophobic surface exposure further show that the non-functional population has altered surface properties relative to the active population. Differences in these properties persist for at least four hours following renaturation, indicating the system remains out-of-equilibrium. Together, these results demonstrate that size exclusion chromatography can be used to isolate soluble, non-aggregating, misfolded states that are structurally similar to the native state yet functionally inactive. This approach provides a basis for enriching such misfolded states for subsequent high-resolution structural characterization.

papers.title: VMDance: An Efficient and Interactive Molecular Dynamics Clustering Plugin for VMD
papers.abstract: Clustering is the standard route from a molecular dynamics trajectory to a small set of interpretable conformational states, yet it is usually performed outside the molecular viewer, leaving cluster assignments to be exported, tracked, and mapped back onto the structures by hand. We present VMDance, an open-source plugin that brings the MDANCE family of $n$-ary similarity clustering methods into VMD. Through a graphical interface backed by a C++ implementation, it provides kmeans{} NANI, HELM, eQual, and DIVINE clustering, together with PRIME representative-structure selection. These methods scale linearly with the number of frames and support deterministic initialization, so partitions can be reproduced exactly and recomputed interactively. Cluster assignments, quality metrics, and representative structures are linked to the loaded trajectory, keeping the analysis of conformational states alongside the structures themselves. VMDance is freely available at url{https://github.com/diegoenry/vmd-mdance-plugin}

papers.title: Beyond the Classical Flake-to-Vesicle Mechanism: Non-standard Vesicles Arise from S-Shaped Intermediates
papers.abstract: Vesicles are indispensable tools across numerous scientific and pharmaceutical fields, however, optimizing their properties necessitates a comprehensive understanding of their formation mechanism. The formation of lipid vesicles from bilayered lipid flakes has long been recognized as a fundamental step in vesicle preparation. The classical flake-to-vesicle mechanism, grounded in continuum models, describes this process as the transformation of a lipid flake into a regular spherical vesicle (RSV) via a cup-shaped intermediate. Nevertheless, this classical mechanism fails to account for emerging experimental observations of non-standard vesicles exhibiting diverse morphologies. Here, using extensive coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations combined with Markov state model analysis, we systematically revisit this transition process at near-atomic resolution. In addition to the standard product, we observe a notable fraction of non-standard vesicles, including small-sized spherical vesicles (SSVs), ellipsoidal vesicles (ELVs), and flake-derived vesicle complexes (FVCs). These non-standard products arise from S-shaped intermediates that differ from the classical cup-shaped intermediate, and the degree of S-shapedness is closely correlated with whether non-standard vesicles are generated and, if so, which specific types. This correlation holds consistently across four lipid systems with distinct compositions and transbilayer distributions. On this basis, we propose a generalized mechanism that explicitly incorporates the S-shaped intermediates and the non-standard vesicles. This new mechanism opens new opportunities for the innovative development of engineered vesicles with tailored morphologies for diagnostics, drug delivery, and therapeutics.

papers.title: Integrating hydrogen-exchange experiments with conformational ensembles
papers.abstract: Protein conformational dynamics are central to biological function but remain difficult to characterise at scale. Amide hydrogen exchange (HX), measured by NMR or mass spectrometry, probes these dynamics but requires computational models for integration with structural ensembles. We benchmark models for calculating HX from ensembles using a large literature-derived dataset spanning folded and intrinsically disordered proteins. We then develop a model that identifies exchange-competent amides from local structural descriptors while accounting for electrostatic effects. The model predicts protection across a broad dynamic range in ensembles generated by molecular dynamics and generative AI. HX-guided ensemble reweighting improves agreement with independent NMR, SAXS, and folding-stability measurements. Millisecond HX distinguishes and refines alternative ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins, while reweighting of structured proteins reveals folding intermediates and low-population excited states. These results establish HX as a quantitative restraint for ensemble reweighting and provide a scalable framework for benchmarking simulations and generative protein models.

papers.title: From Growth Inhibition to Fluctuations: Testing an Ising Model of Bacterial Responses to Antibiotics
papers.abstract: Complex networks of biochemical reactions have been proposed to exhibit emergent cooperativity that can be described by an effective Ising model, with a small number of parameters encoding collective interactions. Here this mapping is experimentally tested using the response of three bacterial species to a range of antibiotics acting on different cellular targets. The Ising description is compared to the conventional Hill model, examining both the mean growth-rate response and, importantly, its population growth-rate heterogeneity (PGRH). While both models describe the mean growth-rate dependence on antibiotic concentration comparably well, we find that the Ising model provides a markedly better description of PGRH, offering an additional and more stringent test of the collective description. The fitted Ising interaction strength is systematically related to the Hill exponent and increases with the functional distance of the antibiotic target from the protein-production machinery. These results provide experimental support for describing complex biochemical reaction networks through effective cooperative Ising interactions, and suggest that the collective response of bacterial growth to antibiotics reflects the organization of the underlying metabolic network.

papers.title: Automated Transcription Factor Cluster Analysis Toolkit (ATAT)
papers.abstract: Many nuclear regulatory proteins, including transcription factors (TFs) form clusters often referred to as hubs or condensates. These clusters vary widely in their enrichment, size, and persistence, yet tools for quantifying these properties are typically developed for individual datasets. Here, we present the Automated TF Cluster Analysis Toolkit (ATAT), a Python-based toolkit for quantifying TF clustering in four-dimensional fluorescence microscopy data. ATAT combines two analytical pipelines: SCAN, which segments nuclear clusters and measures their spatial distribution, enrichment, and persistence, and LOCK, which quantifies TF enrichment and its dynamics at individual genomic loci. Using live Drosophila embryos, we demonstrate that ATAT distinguishes TF clusters from background fluorescence fluctuations across imaging conditions and resolves differences in TF enrichment and persistence at specific genes. ATAT provides a reproducible framework for investigating the spatial and temporal organization of transcriptional regulators in living cells.

papers.title: Hour-long live-cell TIRF imaging of GFP-talin at ensemble and single-molecule level with low-duty-cycle picosecond supercontinuum excitation
papers.abstract: Photobleaching and phototoxicity limit how long living cells can be followed by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy. We describe an objective-type TIRF microscope illuminated by a picosecond supercontinuum laser spectrally windowed to 20-nm bands, pulse-picked to 1 MHz and delivered through two TIRF illuminators, one per polarisation direction. Single GFP-talin molecules in focal adhesions of living cells were detected throughout uninterrupted recordings of 10-31 min, and drift-corrected, time-stamped localisations resolved adhesion motion of tens of nanometres per minute. In diffraction-limited time-lapse at one frame per second, adhesion brightness, adhesion area, cell footprint and adhesion motility were unchanged after an hour. Under continuous-wave excitation on a comparable commercial TIRF microscope, the same schedule preserved cell behaviour at a low laser setting but adhesions dimmed, and higher settings bleached and retracted cells within a minute of exposure. We provide the datasets and open ImageJ tools for drift correction and localisation.

papers.title: Determination of both global and local protein stability in complex environments with X-ray hydroxyl radical footprinting
papers.abstract: Protein thermodynamic stability is a major determinant of cellular function, yet traditional methods for determining protein stability require large quantities of pure protein under idealized conditions. Here, we overcome this challenge by combining X-ray hydroxyl radical footprinting monitored by mass spectrometry (XF-MS) with chemical denaturation, to accurately measure protein thermodynamic stability. We demonstrate that XF-MS quantitatively reproduces known stability values using ~500-fold less protein than traditional spectroscopic approaches such as circular dichroism. Detection with mass spectrometry extends these measurements to heterogeneous samples demonstrated by measuring the stability of individual proteins in complex mixtures, including in cell lysate. Furthermore, by monitoring XF-MS at the level of individual peptides, we can monitor local stability and detect deviations from the typical assumed two-state unfolding behavior. This local resolution allows us to detect distinct cooperative units and assign thermodynamic values to individual structural domains within a multi-domain protein. In sum, XF-MS extends quantitative stability measurements to a broader range of proteins, environments, and levels of structural detail than previously accessible with conventional approaches.

papers.title: EM-Claw: An Experience-Grounded Language-Model Agent for Auto Cryo-EM Single-Particle Analysis
papers.abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) processing remains strongly dependent on expert judgement because difficult specimens often require dataset-specific strategies that cannot be captured by a fixed pipeline. Here we present EM-Claw, an experience-grounded multi-agent system for adaptive cryo-EM single-particle analysis. Rather than following a predefined workflow, EM-Claw retrieves processing precedents from previously solved datasets, consults external guidance, proposes and independently evaluates alternative strategies, executes CryoSPARC or RELION jobs, and revises the processing route according to quantitative and visual evidence. Human expertise can be introduced at any stage through natural-language instructions, while successful decisions and processing trajectories are retained as reusable experience. We evaluated EM-Claw on both publicly available cryo-EM datasets and experimental datasets collected in our laboratory, spanning soluble proteins, membrane proteins, GPCR complexes and small transporter monomers. Across these cases, EM-Claw adapted its processing strategies to specimen-specific challenges, including compositional heterogeneity, complex flexibility, preferred orientation and weak particle features. It produced reconstructions at higher resolution than previously published results (0.1~1.3 angstroms improvement) or solved structures that are now being prepared for publication, with no or little human intervention, thereby substantially reducing the time, effort and field experience required for human decision-making.

papers.title: Synovial Fluid Spatial Microrheology is Shaped by Extracellular Matrix Identity and Mucin Integrity
papers.abstract: The interfacial organization of synovial fluid (SF) contributes to cartilage protection and lubrication, yet how articular cartilage extracellular matrix (AC-ECM) identity influences the rheological response of supramolecularly assembled SF films remains to be elucidated. Here, depth-resolved multiple-particle tracking microrheology was used to examine diluted SF (dSF) near immobilized collagen type II (Col-II), collagen type I (Col-I), and fibronectin (FN). Untreated dSF exhibited increased relative apparent viscosity near Col-II and FN, whereas the response near Col-I was comparatively negligible. Treatment with StcE, a mucin-selective protease previously shown to cleave lubricin's mucin domain in SF, resulted in more pronounced effects of the interface on the depth dependent viscosity profiles across all three substrates. Analysis of the complex modulus and viscosity revealed significant effects with depth changes and StcE treatment. Quartz crystal microbalance measurements further revealed that the adsorbed amount of the fluids onto AC-ECM substrates did not directly correspond to the magnitude of microrheological modulation, with Col-I showing limited retention despite a pronounced near-interface response following StcE treatment. Together, these findings indicate that AC-ECM identity and StcE-sensitive SF constituents are associated with spatial variations in viscoelasticity that are not directly reflected by far-field tracer dynamics or interfacial adsorption alone.

papers.title: Intrinsically disordered regions within transcription factors impact DNA binding through both autoinhibition and independent DNA binding
papers.abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) recognize DNA through structured DNA-binding domains (DBDs), but the contributions of their flanking intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) to DNA binding remain poorly understood. Here, we dissected how IDRs impact DNA binding in vitro by investigating three paralogous Saccharomyces cerevisiae TFs with highly similar DNA-binding domains but divergent IDRs (Msn2, Msn4, and Com2). Using high-throughput microfluidic binding assays, we quantified >17,000,000 TF-DNA relative binding energies between Msn2, Msn4, and Com2 variant constructs and DNA libraries comprised of systematic substitutions or genomic sequences. These measurements reveal that IDRs do not alter core 'motif' specificities but alter DNA binding affinities via two distinct mechanisms. First, the Msn2 and Msn4 IDRs autoinhibit their cognate DBDs, imposing a uniform free-energy penalty that depends on the combination of DNA-binding domain and IDR. Second, di-arginine pairs within the Msn2 IDR selectively bind low-complexity, homopolymeric DNA with very weak affinities only detectable under avid binding conditions. Neural-network models trained on in vivo Msn2 binding data (ChEC-seq) reveal similar preferences for clustered homopolymeric sequences, suggesting this weak binding impacts genomic localization in cells via intermolecular avidity. These results establish that IDRs influence TF-DNA binding through diverse mechanisms operating both independently of and in concert with DBD motif recognition.

papers.title: Mechanical and Interfacial Coupling in Bacterial Biofilm Detachment Underwater
papers.abstract: Biofilms form persistent surface-associated communities across natural, industrial, and biomedical environments and cause significant socioeconomic distress, yet their controlled removal remains challenging, especially in wet and underwater conditions. Inspired by barnacle adhesives that clear underlying biomass before their permanent attachment, here we introduce adhesive peeling as a readily adoptable, practical strategy for controlled removal and characterization of biofilms underwater. Using underwater adhesives, force-controlled contact peeling, and in situ confocal microscopy, we show that bacterial biofilms can be transferred from submerged surfaces to an adhesive, with removal reaching ~ 82%. Additionally, with a mechano-interfacial map that combines underwater biofilm-adhesive work of adhesion and biofilm-adhesive mechanical mismatch, we found three distinct species-dependent adhesive peeling mechanisms: (i) E. coli peeling is dominated by favorable interfacial interactions and is insensitive to adhesive mechanics, (ii) S. aureus peeling requires a balance between interfacial affinity and mechanical response, and (iii) P. aeruginosa peeling is insensitive to adhesive identity, consistent with cohesion-limited failure within the biofilm. These results establish adhesive peeling as a methodology for both removing biofilms and identifying the dominant failure pathway within submerged adhesive-biofilm-substrate-water interfaces, providing a physical basis for understanding how living biofilms contact, adhere, and fail against non-living materials across healthcare, transportation, and industrial systems where persistent biofouling carries substantial human and economic costs.

papers.title: A Single Kinetic Parameter Determines Intermediate Filament Elongation
papers.abstract: Intermediate filaments elongate by end-to-end annealing of filament subunits. We develop a Smoluchowski coagulation model with a single kinetic parameter, k0, that reproduces data from time-resolved atomic force microscopy, electron microscopy, and static light scattering. The model predicts log-normal filament length distributions, sublinear filament growth, and saturation of scattering intensity ratios. For a given protein, the inferred assembly rate constants agree across measurement techniques

papers.title: Automating Glycosylation of Protein Models in the Martini 3 Force Field with GlycoMarinate
papers.abstract: Most membrane and secreted proteins undergo glycosylation, the covalent posttranslational addition of oligosaccharide chains. Glycans, which constitute up to 30% of a glycoprotein's mass, alter protein trafficking, dynamics, interactions, and thus function. Because of their heterogeneity, rapid dynamics, and conformational richness, glycans are difficult to characterise experimentally, so molecular simulations can provide a powerful alternative for studying their effects on proteins. Given that the time and length scales involved are typically large, coarse-grained models can be used to enhance the sampling and allow for the study of interactions of glycoproteins in their cellular context. Although individual saccharides and glycans have been parameterised for coarse-grained simulations, modelling new glycan structures has largely required system-specific parameter development, and no general framework connects transferable glycan models with automated construction of complete glycoproteins. Here, we introduce GlycoMarinate, a general framework for coarse-grained modelling of N-glycoproteins within the Martini 3 force field. The framework supports two complementary levels of glycan description: a transferable generic model designed for broad applicability, and refined glycan-specific models optimised against atomistic conformational ensembles. We derive and validate refined models for ten representative high-mannose, hybrid, and complex N-glycans. Both descriptions are integrated into an automated workflow that generates the topologies and clash-free starting coordinates for site-specifically glycosylated proteins. We demonstrate the framework on biologically relevant systems, including the densely glycosylated SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.

papers.title: Hierarchical Matrix Compression for Fast BidomainSimulation of Multicellular Neuron Models
papers.abstract: The bidomain boundary element-cable method (Cable-BEM) couples the intracellular, membrane, and extracellular dynamics of multicellular neuron models using only the compartmental unknowns of cable models. However, its matrices are dense, and their storage and factorization scale as O(N2) and O(N3) for N unknowns, respectively. We compare four hierarchical matrix formats for compressing these matrices: hierarchically off-diagonal low-rank (HODLR), hierarchically semiseparable (HSS), H-matrices, and H2-matrices. For a layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron, the four formats use 2.7 to 6.1 times less memory than the dense solver. At a tolerance of 10-3, the maximum membrane potential errors are 8.5 mV for HSS, 0.47 mV for HODLR, and at most 10-3 mV for the H- and H2-matrices. For arrays of 9 to 225 parallel axons (1,827 to 45,675 unknowns), the maximum rank reaches 1,759 for HSS and 797 for HODLR, whereas it remains at or below 101 for the H- and H2-matrices. These results suggest that H- and H2-matrices scale more favorably than HODLR and HSS for networks of closely packed cells.

papers.title: Robust parameter estimation and dose-fractionation for ptychographic single-particle analysis at near-atomic resolution
papers.abstract: We present a complete workflow for the determination of biomolecular structures by single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy using ptychography. To account for the prominent dose damage in biological specimens dose-fractionated data acquisition and processing are introduced. Automated preprocessing techniques estimate the probe shape and scanning geometry before the ptychographic reconstruction by utilising the shadow image inside the Ronchigram. Standard ptychographic single-particle analysis is performed using tobacco mosaic virus, apoferritin and hepatitis B virus capsids. We finally give a demonstration of dose-fractionated ptychography utilising multiple scans of the same area at low dose reaching near-atomic resolution (3.3 [A]), allowing for the automated building of atomic models.

papers.title: The mechanism of regulation of prokaryotic Na+ channels by their C-terminal domain
papers.abstract: Prokaryotic voltage-gated Na+-channels (BacNaVs) closely resemble neuronal NaV channels in their structure and gating behavior and are found in multiple bacterial lineages, yet little is known about their biological function. In NaVSp1 from the marine bacterium Ruegeria pomeroyi, the cytoplasmic C-terminal domain (CTD) was proposed to function as a temperature sensor. Here, we use electrophysiology and computational methods to establish how the CTD can tune the temperature- and voltage-dependence of the NaVSp1 channel. We show that although the CTD of NaVSp1 is not a temperature sensor, its conformational dynamics are directly coupled to the gating of the pore. Additionally, we find that interactions between the CTD and the transmembrane domain can reduce or completely suppress the response of NaVSp1 to temperature by stabilizing the open state of the channel. Although BacNaV channels share low sequence identity in their CTDs, we provide evidence suggesting that most are structurally similar to NaVSp1 through the mining and modeling of more than 800 sequences from distinct bacteria. The mechanism we described could therefore be important for BacNaV channel regulation in response to environmental factors like temperature in a wide number of bacterial species.

papers.title: Free-edge mechanics and hydrodynamic coupling shape membrane remodeling after pore opening
papers.abstract: Membrane remodeling after pore opening occurs in electroporation, vesicle rupture, intracellular delivery, and pathogen escape from host cells. During this process, a pore may expand or close while the surrounding membrane curls at the rim, forms a neck, or everts. Using a sharp-interface framework for open membranes in Stokes flow, we study how free-edge elasticity and the dissipation mechanism determine post-opening remodeling. The model combines Helfrich bending, Gaussian-curvature and line energies, and local area inextensibility with viscous dissipation in the membrane and the surrounding fluid. We compare it with a local-drag model driven by the same energy over a range of line tensions, Gaussian rigidities, and spontaneous curvatures. Starting from a spherical cap, the membrane first adjusts near the rim as it relaxes toward the free-edge moment condition. The subsequent pore dynamics depend strongly on line tension, with trajectories that either continue to expand or reverse and shrink. Gaussian rigidity changes the rim orientation; for positive Gaussian rigidity, a pronounced internal neck develops behind an outward-moving free edge. Increasingly negative spontaneous curvature localizes deformation near the rim and, at sufficiently negative values, causes the first complete rim turn to precede cap inversion. Hydrodynamic and local-drag simulations can dissipate similar amounts of energy while following different shape trajectories, so in the strongly curved regime the pathway depends on the dissipation model as well as on the energy. Together, the edge tangent angle, neck radius, cap depth, and the relative timing of rim rolling and cap inversion provide measurable geometric signatures that distinguish post-opening remodeling pathways beyond the pore radius.

papers.title: On the Importance of Polarizability in Simulations of 2D IR Spectra of the Potassium Ion Channel KcsA
papers.abstract: The bacterial KcsA channel is a K+ channel which is functionally homologous to mammalian ion channels. It assembles as a cone-shaped tetramer that is embedded in the membrane. Its narrowest conserved region, known as the selectivity filter (SF) is comprised of five distinct ion-binding sites (S0-S4) that coordinate the selective permeation of K+ ions. Recent two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) spectroscopy experiments, together with molecular dynamics and line shape simulations on the isotope-labeled SF residues V76 and G77, suggest that in the closed conductive state either S1/S3 or S2/S4 are occupied by ions with water molecules in between, consistent with the soft knock-on mechanism. 2D IR spectroscopy probes amide I vibrations that are highly sensitive to local environmental fluctuations thus providing a powerful approach for distinguishing ion permeation mechanisms. However, current 2D IR spectral calculations are largely restricted to non-polarizable force fields, which may not fully capture the realistic channel behavior. Here, we report 2D IR simulations based on all-atom molecular dynamics trajectories of the KcsA channel embedded in a lipid membrane performed using nonpolarizable CHARMM36m, polarizable CHARMM-Drude, and CHARMM force field with electronic continuum correction. The spectra were calculated for V76 and G77 isotope-labeled SF and for soft knock-on configurations. Our results show that simulations with the polarizable CHARMM-Drude force field better reproduce experimental 2D IR spectra underscoring the importance of including the polarization effects in simulations of ion channels.

papers.title: Structural and Biophysical Basis of the First DNA Aptamer Targeting the Dynamic p47 Adaptor of the p97 AAA+ Machine
papers.abstract: Selective modulation of dynamic proteins within native multiprotein assemblies remains a major challenging for chemical biology. Here, we develop p47A1, the first DNA aptamer targeting the p97 adaptor p47 (NSFL1C) and uncover an unexpected allosteric mechanism of action. Target-immobilized SELEX identifies a highly convergent aptamer whose conformation is stabilized by Mg2+. Our comprehensive structural and biophysical characterization shows that p47A1 recognizes the SEP domain and adjacent SIM-SEP linker of p47 with low-micromolar affinity. Rather than simply occupying the p47 surface, aptamer binding remodels the intramolecular regulatory architecture of p47, disrupting intramolecular contacts and releasing the UBA domain into a highly dynamic state. Site-specific fluorescent labeling and mutational studies define the aptamer binding site. Importantly, reconstitution studies demonstrate that the aptamer engages p47 within the intact p47-p97 complex without disrupting the native complex or the basal p97 ATPase activity. Together, p47A1 provides a precise chemical biology probe for p47 and illustrates the potential of aptamers to target dynamic regulatory adaptors within native AAA+ protein assemblies.

papers.title: Purification and structural characterisation of mRNA monomers, dimers, and multimers using atomic force microscopy
papers.abstract: mRNA has emerged as an important new class of medicines, offering new opportunities as vaccines and therapeutics. mRNA molecules are large, highly polar and fold into complex, higher-order structures, resulting in heterogeneity. Multimerisation (aggregation) is a critical quality attribute of mRNA and may affect translational efficiency or lipid nanoparticle formulation. However, mRNA multimerisation remains poorly studied, as robust analytical methods are required for characterisation and structurally distinct populations are difficult to isolate for downstream analysis. We have developed and utilised preparative-scale, non-denaturing ion-pair reversed-phase HPLC to purify distinct mRNA monomer, dimer and multimer populations. Downstream desalting using tangential flow filtration ensured no significant perturbation of purified mRNA populations. Further characterisation of the mRNA higher-order structures was performed using Atomic Force Microscopy and subsequent automated structural analysis. mRNA dimers/multimers formed structured higher-order assemblies rather than end-to-end elongations, with mRNAs maintaining a distinct shape, even during multimerisation. Purifying distinct mRNA monomer, dimer and multimer populations establishes a platform for detailed structural, biochemical and biophysical analysis of higher-order mRNA structures. These methodologies provide insight into complex mRNA secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Integrating these approaches with design strategies to enhance mRNA stability and protein expression will accelerate the development of next-generation mRNA therapeutics
